name: Suction cup / cupping on cheeks
lead: Cupping on the cheeks is the use of small suction cups on the face, borrowed from the wider practice of cupping therapy, with the aim of shaping or refreshing the cheek area. Practitioners create a partial vacuum in a cup placed on the skin so that tissue is drawn gently into it, and people who try it on the face do so hoping for a fuller-looking, livelier or more contoured cheek.[1]

In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the technique is discussed as a low-cost, at-home way to work on facial appearance. Proponents describe the suction as stimulating circulation in the skin, which they associate with a healthier-looking complexion and a lifted look. Cupping on the body has been used in many traditions, and the face version is an adaptation of it.

Cupping in general leaves circular marks where capillaries beneath the skin respond to the suction. A 2020 eye-tracking study of cupping marks found that people notice and attend to these marks, which is one reason facial cupping is often done with light suction and short sessions.[2] No published trials have tested cheek cupping for cosmetic results.

chain: Suction cup draws cheek skin into the cup
Temporary flush and lift in the area
angle.text: People use small suction cups on the cheeks hoping for a temporary lift, a flush of color and a more contoured look. The effect described by users is short-lived and tied to the suction session itself.

card.summary: Small suction cups applied to the cheeks to draw up the skin for a temporary flushed, lifted look.
card.note: Suction can leave temporary round marks on the skin.

quick.overview:
Facial cupping uses small suction cups on the cheeks. Users hope it gives a fuller, more lifted and more colorful cheek area, and it is usually done in short sessions with light suction.

It is an offshoot of traditional body cupping, adapted for the face. Results people describe are temporary, and no published trials have tested it for cheek shaping.
quick.mechanism: A cup creates a partial vacuum that pulls skin and underlying tissue upward into it. This briefly brings blood to the surface, which proponents link to a flushed, lifted look.
quick.risks: Suction can break tiny capillaries and leave circular marks or bruises, and strong suction on thin facial skin is where most reported marks come from. Cupping is generally regarded as suitable for most people when done by trained practitioners, but conditions such as eczema or psoriasis can be aggravated.

paras: Cups used on the face are typically small silicone or plastic cups that are squeezed or pumped to create suction, in contrast to the larger glass or bamboo cups used on the back. Cupping therapy more broadly includes dry cupping (suction only), fire cupping, and wet cupping.[1]

Facial cupping is discussed as a do-it-yourself approach to cheek definition and skin glow. Users describe moving the cup across the cheek or holding it briefly in place. Because the marks cupping can leave are visible, users commonly describe keeping suction light on the face.[2]

Suction breaks small capillaries under the skin, which produces circular bruises or petechiae. Other reported risks of cupping include burns with fire cupping, skin discoloration, and flare-ups of eczema or psoriasis.[1] Research on how people react to cupping marks shows they draw visual attention, which is relevant on the face.[2]
No studies found. Studies of cupping therapy on the body have examined mainly pain conditions and are described in reviews as variable in quality.[1]
